paras: The attempted lynching of William Beaner was a night ride by a party of horsemen on the Loudoun County jail at Leesburg, Virginia, on 7 September 1882, aimed at seizing and lynching a Black youth held there. The riders reached the jail, met the jailor and his sons, and turned back without trying to enter, and Beaner was not harmed. Local papers treated the failed raid with derision or, in one case, regret that the sheriff had been ready.

According to the Loudoun Telephone, on Tuesday evening, 5 September, the daughter of George Hunt, a deaf girl of about ten living near Alder's schoolhouse, was walking visiting children home when she was assaulted in a piece of woods. The paper named the attacker as "a colored boy named William Beaner," about eighteen, who had been working nearby, and stated the accusation as fact. Drawn by the other children's screams, Hunt and other men chased the youth through a cornfield and found him hiding in a barn's haymow, and on Wednesday Justice Grubb took him to jail. The Clarke Courier placed the Hunt home near Purcellville and named the jail as the one at Leesburg.

On Thursday the sheriff learned, according to the Leesburg Washingtonian, that a party had been organized in the neighborhood of the alleged crime to take the prisoner from the jail that night and lynch him. He placed pickets on the roads into town, and around midnight they reported a large body of horsemen coming down the Leesburg turnpike, so he went to ring the courthouse bell to call out the citizens.

Before he returned, a first squad of about twenty riders, some with faces covered, came down Market Street from the Fair Ground and halted in front of the jail, where the jailor and his sons met them. The Washingtonian wrote that not a man dismounted and not a word was spoken before the squad turned and rode back out Market Street. A second squad then came up the Alexandria pike from the east and rode through town without halting, by which time citizens had gathered.
The paper put the whole party at forty or fifty and reported that the riders' only other act was to hold a Leesburg citizen under guard in the road near the Fair Ground until they had come and gone.
No one was reported identified or charged for the ride, and the coverage does not show any indictment, trial or later disposition of the charge against Beaner.

The story reached readers through two Leesburg weeklies, the Telephone and the Washingtonian, whose accounts were reprinted in other Virginia papers within a week. The Richmond Dispatch ran the Telephone's account of the accusation and arrest in a state-news column on 10 September, without mention of the ride. The Alexandria Gazette printed both papers on 11 September under the headline "Outrage-a Fizzle," and its Washingtonian text mocked the raiders' "farce" as "more a midnight frolic than a serious attempt at lynching" while crediting the sheriff with maintaining the law.

The Clarke Courier of Berryville took the opposite view on 14 September, calling the accused "the wretch" and writing that "unfortunately the sheriff had gotten wind of their coming." All three papers reported the assault as established fact rather than an accusation, and the Courier gave the youth's name as "Wm. Beauer."

accounts.label: Leesburg Washingtonian
accounts.gist: The sheriff learned of the plan and prepared; about twenty riders came to the jail, faced the jailor and his sons, and left without a word; a second squad rode by. It judged the ride 'more a midnight frolic than a serious attempt at lynching.'

accounts.label: Clarke Courier
accounts.gist: Summarizes the Washingtonian, calls the accused 'the wretch', and regrets that the sheriff was ready to resist.
